c1.story:
Retail sounds like one business: buy goods, put them on a shelf, sell them for more. But spend a Saturday in any Indian city and you will walk through four businesses that share almost nothing except a cash counter.

Start at DMart. The aisles are plain, the queues are long, and the prices are the lowest in town on the things you buy every week. Radhakishan Damani built it on a counter-intuitive idea: own the store instead of renting it, keep the range narrow, pay suppliers quickly and pass every saving on to the shopper. The margin on each packet of dal is tiny. The trick is how many packets leave the store per square foot, every day, for years. Vishal Mega Mart runs a similar value playbook for clothes and general merchandise in smaller towns.

Now walk into a Zudio. Everything is the chain's own brand, priced so a college student can buy a full outfit without a second thought. Trent built Zudio into one of the fastest-growing chains in the country, and the economics are the opposite of a grocer's: a high markup on its own designs, as long as the clothes sell at full price before the season ends. Metro's shoe stores, Manyavar's wedding sherwanis and the Louis Philippe and Van Heusen shelves of Aditya Birla Lifestyle Brands live behind the same door.

Then the jeweller. At Kalyan or Thangamayil you pay for gold by weight, at the day's price, plus a making charge. The gold itself is a pass-through; the chain earns on the making charge and, above all, on trust. Nobody hands their daughter's wedding budget to a shop they do not trust.

And finally the wholesaler in the back lane: Redington moving phones and laptops, SG Mart moving steel, Sky Gold making jewellery for the chains. Their margins are razor thin and their skill is cash, collecting from dealers faster than they pay suppliers.

Same word, four businesses: one sells cheapness, one sells taste, one sells trust and one sells speed of cash.
c1.read:
The four tiles are the four doors. Read each from top to bottom, then compare the profit bars across the row.

  • The name and the line under it tell you where the profit comes from: volume and owned stores for value grocery; design and full-price selling for fashion and footwear; trust and the making charge for jewellery; working capital discipline for distributors.
  • The tickers are listed names that mostly sit behind that door. Click one to open its stock page.
  • The profit bar is the part to compare. Fashion and footwear sits at high: own brands, high markups. Value grocery sits at medium, which surprises people given its thin margins; the bar reflects how efficiently it turns stock and capital, not the margin per packet. Jewellery sits at medium too, because gold passes through at cost and only the making charge is profit. Distributors sit at low.
  • The last line is the bet: store growth and lowest prices, brand heat and full-price sell-through, weddings and the shift to chains, or volumes with tight working capital.

The analogy below gives you a picture for each: the cheap busy kirana, the boutique, the family jeweller, the back-lane wholesaler. The so-what line is the discipline: compare a name only with its own door. A grocer's thin gross margin next to a fashion chain's fat one tells you nothing about which is the better business. What matters is how each turns its margin into return on capital.

c2.story:
Follow a kurta from the loom to your wardrobe and you have the retail kitchen. It was stitched in a garment unit in Tiruppur or Bangladesh. It moved in bulk to a warehouse. A distribution centre sorted it with thousands of others and put it on a truck to a store. You walked into that store, or tapped an app, and bought it. That is five stations, and every retail format walks a version of it.

The first station belongs to the makers: FMCG companies, garment mills, gold refiners and importers, phone brands, many of them Chinese. Retailers rarely make what they sell, though the fashion chains increasingly design it and contract out the stitching.

The second station is wholesale and distribution, and this is where the listed distributors stand. Redington takes phones and laptops from brands to thousands of dealers. SG Mart moves steel. Sky Gold makes and supplies jewellery to the chains. Pearl Global stitches garments for global brands.

The third station is the one shoppers never see and the one that decides who wins: the supply chain. DMart, Trent and Vishal Mega Mart run their own distribution centres. A grocer that can restock every store daily, without piling up inventory, can afford lower prices than a rival who cannot.

The fourth station is the store or the app, where the retailer meets you. And here is the shift of the last few years: at that station, a new kind of rival now stands. Blinkit, Zepto and Swiggy Instamart deliver groceries in minutes from dark stores, warehouses that look like shops but let no shoppers in. Amazon and Flipkart sell almost everything else.

One fact frames the whole picture: organised retail still holds well under a fifth of Indian retail. The rest is kiranas and local shops. That is why the listed chains can grow for years simply by taking share, and why the fight with the apps is about who takes that share.
c2.read:
The diagram has two layers. Read the top row left to right, then the two band rows underneath.

The five boxes are the stations: makers and sourcing, distribution and wholesale, warehousing and supply chain, stores and apps, and the household. Each box says what happens there and who stands there. Notice that the listed distributors appear at station two, while DMart, Trent and Vishal Mega Mart appear at both station three and station four. Owning the supply chain behind the store is the hallmark of the best Indian chains.

The first band row shows who holds each station. The coloured Indian-listed cells run across stations two, three and four, more of the chain than in most consumer industries. Station four's cell reads Indian listed plus apps, a reminder that the shop floor is now shared.

The second band row shows where the rival stands: quick-commerce and online platforms. Their name repeats across the first four stations, with the household cell left to the wider world. That is the point of the picture. The apps are not a rival at one station; they are an alternative route through the whole chain, buying from makers, running their own dark-store warehouses and selling straight to your door.

Then read the note: organised retail is still well under a fifth of the total, growth has moved to small towns where rents are lower and branded stores are new, and jewellery is strongest in the south. The so-what line gives the tension in one sentence: a long runway of share to take from local shops, and a new rival competing for it in urban grocery and impulse buys.

c3.story:
Retail is the most honest read on the Indian household wallet. Not the wallet in a survey, the wallet at the till. And that wallet belongs to six quite different shoppers.

The urban middle-class household is the core: groceries every week, fashion and footwear every season, a phone or laptop every few years. It moves with salaries, income-tax changes and food inflation. When vegetables and dal get expensive, the family does not eat less. It postpones the second pair of jeans.

The small-town household is where the growth is. Many families there are making their first branded purchase, walking into a Zudio or a Vishal Mega Mart that opened down the road last year. Their spending follows farm income and rural wages, but it also follows the store itself: in a town with no organised store, a new opening creates demand that was not visible before.

Then the occasion shoppers. Wedding families buy gold jewellery, ethnic wear and footwear, and they buy on dates fixed by the priest, not the economy. A season with many auspicious wedding dates is a strong quarter for Kalyan and Manyavar, whatever the GDP print says. Festive shoppers crowd into Navratri, Dhanteras and Diwali, so a Diwali that falls in late October rather than November can move sales from one quarter to the next.

The young urban shopper chases fast fashion, sneakers and, increasingly, lab-grown diamonds, and discovers most of it on social media. And the dealers and resellers who buy from the distributors respond to product launch cycles, construction activity and export orders, which makes the distributors a different animal from the shop-floor retailers.

The sequence matters. When food inflation eats salaries, fashion slows first, jewellery follows, and groceries slow last. When inflation eases, the order reverses.

When dal gets dearer, the family still eats. It postpones the second pair of jeans.
c3.read:
Each tile is one customer group. Read every tile in three lines.

  • The name is who is buying.
  • The second line is what they buy from this industry.
  • The third line is what moves them, which is your watch list outside the industry.

Now sort the tiles into three groups. The everyday wallet: urban and small-town households, moved by salaries, taxes, food inflation and farm income. The calendar wallet: wedding families and festive shoppers, moved by auspicious dates, Diwali timing and bonuses. And the business wallet: dealers and resellers, moved by product launches and construction.

Each group maps to a door from card one. Grocery leans on the everyday wallet. Fashion and footwear lean on the everyday wallet plus the young shopper. Jewellery leans heavily on the calendar wallet and the gold price. Distributors lean on the business wallet, which is why they rarely move with the consumer cycle at all.

Two practical uses. First, before judging a quarter, check the calendar: a jeweller's weak quarter may simply mean the wedding dates fell in the next one. Second, read the so-what line as a ranking of sensitivity: fashion slows first when food inflation bites, groceries last. If you hold a fashion chain, food inflation is your most important number even though you sell no food.

c4.story:
Retail profit has a shape you can almost feel. It is a small margin multiplied by speed.

Take a value grocer. Out of every hundred rupees a shopper spends, more than four-fifths go straight back to the suppliers who made the goods. Staff, rent, power and marketing take a small slice, kept small by obsessive discipline. Depreciation and interest are slim too. What is left is a sliver, only a few rupees. How does anyone get rich on that? By doing it fast. A grocer turns its stock over every few weeks, so the same capital earns that sliver again and again through the year. DMart adds a twist: it owns most of its stores, so there is no landlord to raise the rent, and it pays suppliers quickly in exchange for better prices.

Now take a fashion chain. The goods cost a bit over half of sales, because the chain designs its own clothes and sets its own markup. But it spends far more on stores, staff, rent and marketing, about a quarter of sales, because a fashion store must look good and sit where shoppers walk. Depreciation and interest are heavier too, because a fashion chain usually leases its stores, and since lease accounting changed in 2019, that rent shows up as depreciation and interest. What is left is roughly double the grocer's slice.

Then the line that ruins retailers: inventory. A grocer holds weeks of stock. A fashion chain holds months, and if the season's designs miss, the only way out is a discount that eats the margin. A jeweller holds months of gold, financed partly with gold loans, which is why the gold price is both a revenue engine and a balance-sheet risk.

A grocer gets rich on a sliver by doing it fast. A fashion chain gets rich on a fat margin, until the season goes wrong.

The last test is the new store. Every opening is capex, and the speed at which it pays back decides whether a growth model compounds or quietly bleeds.
c4.read:
The two bar charts walk a hundred rupees of sales down to what is left, for value grocery and for fashion and footwear. Start at the left of each and move right.

  • The first bar is the full hundred rupees.
  • The input bar here is the cost of goods sold, what the retailer paid for what it sold. In the grocery chart it swallows more than four-fifths. In the fashion chart, a bit over half. That gap is the difference between selling other people's brands and selling your own.
  • The opex bar is staff, rent, power and marketing. Grocery's is small, a disciplined single-digit slice. Fashion's is about a quarter.
  • The depreciation and interest bar is slim for grocery and noticeably larger for fashion, because leased stores sit here under lease accounting.
  • The last bar is what is left: a sliver for grocery, roughly double that for fashion.

These are illustrative mid-cycle shapes, not any company's accounts. Hover a bar for the rupee amount. Remember that the grocer's sliver comes round many times a year, which the chart cannot show.

Below, the list marks which P&L lines matter. Gross margin, same-store sales, inventory, rent and capex all get a clear yes, more yeses than most industries, because retail is an operating business through and through. Depreciation, interest and gold hedging get a sometimes, each relevant to one door. The so-what line is the habit: read same-store sales and inventory days together. Rising sales with lean stock is healthy; growth from new stores alone can hide a tired format.

c5.story:
Retail has two clocks ticking at once. The slow one is structural: organised chains taking share from local shops, year after year, regardless of the economy. The fast one is the household mood, and it swings.

The fast clock went haywire in 2020. Lockdowns shut fashion and jewellery stores entirely; only grocery stayed open. Then came the rebound. In 2021 and 2022 Indians went revenge shopping, and a backlog of postponed weddings landed all at once. Jewellery and fashion boomed. Trent's Zudio became the fastest-growing chain in India, opening stores at a pace the industry had not seen.

The peak, in 2022, was as much about valuations as sales. Retail stocks traded at extreme multiples and every chain announced aggressive expansion. Then the bill arrived. Through 2023 and 2024, food inflation ate into household budgets, fashion and footwear same-store sales stalled, and discounting crept back. At the same time, quick-commerce apps grew fast and began taking urban grocery baskets. 2024 was the bottom: weak footfall, inventory corrections, and expansion slowing everywhere except at the leaders.

Then policy turned the fast clock. The February 2025 Union Budget made income up to twelve lakh rupees effectively tax-free under the new regime, putting money directly into salaried pockets. The September 2025 GST cut lowered rates on clothes and daily goods. Gold hit record after record, which lifted jewellery revenue even as buyers bought fewer grams. Vishal Mega Mart and new jewellery chains such as Bluestone arrived on the market.

So today the clock reads early up-cycle. Festive demand has been strong after the tax relief, and store openings are accelerating in small towns. The fly in the ointment is in the metros, where quick commerce keeps squeezing big-box grocery.
c5.read:
Three pieces work together: the clock, the timeline and the four hands.

The clock has four arcs, boom, peak, bust and bottom, clockwise from the top. The years under each show when the last cycle passed through it: boom across 2021 and 2022, peak in 2022, bust through 2023 and 2024, bottom in 2024. The arrow points just past the bottom into the start of the boom arc, labelled early up-cycle, with the detail that tax cuts help and apps compete. Hover an arc to read what defined it.

The timeline retells the cycle from 2019, coloured by tone. Notice two bust-coloured entries: 2020, when stores were simply shut, and 2023 to 2024, when wallets were squeezed. They are very different kinds of bust, one forced, one chosen by the shopper.

The four hands move the arrow.

  • Same-store sales growth: recovering, up arrow. The single best sign of real demand.
  • Food inflation: moderate, up arrow. The arrow points up because moderate inflation is good news here: it frees wallets for fashion and gold.
  • Gold price: near record, a mixed reading. Higher gold lifts jewellery revenue but cuts grams sold.
  • Quick-commerce growth: very fast, down arrow. More pressure on urban grocery.

Two ups, one mixed, one down. Read the arrows as good or bad for the industry, not as the direction of the number itself. The so-what line tells you who benefits first: fashion and value formats, while urban grocery faces a structural new rival.

c6.story:
What decides whether an Indian retailer has a good quarter? Less the retailer than the price of tomatoes and the price of gold.

The first three-dot dial is food inflation, and its channel is subtle. Grocers sell food, so you might expect inflation to help them through higher ticket sizes. But the bigger effect is on everything else: when food takes a bigger bite of the household budget, there is less left for clothes, shoes and jewellery. Food inflation is the fashion retailer's most important number even though it sells no food.

The second three-dot dial is gold, and it is two-faced. A higher gold price lifts a jeweller's revenue, because jewellery is priced by weight at the day's rate. But it cuts the grams people buy: a family with a fixed wedding budget buys a lighter necklace. It also raises the value of the jeweller's inventory, which is pleasant until gold falls. That is why the gold row carries a diamond, not an arrow.

Then come the two-dot dials. Income-tax and GST changes move disposable income and sticker prices, and the February 2025 tax cut and September 2025 GST cut are the clearest recent examples. Wage growth moves footfall and ticket size. And quick-commerce growth, which the table treats as a dial in its own right, steals grocery and impulse purchases from the big stores whenever it accelerates.

The single-dot dials are background. Interest rates matter through EMIs and consumer credit. Commercial rents squeeze leased stores, which is why owning stores is DMart's quiet advantage. Cotton and polyester prices nudge garment costs. And factory output of consumer non-durables is a rough proxy for daily household consumption.

Food inflation is the fashion retailer's most important number, even though it sells no food.
c6.read:
Each row is one dial. Read across in four steps.

  • Dial: the outside force.
  • Channel: how it reaches profits. For retail most channels run through the household wallet: what is left for discretionary purchases, disposable income, spending power, EMIs. A few run through costs: rent and garment inputs.
  • A rise does: the effect of the dial going up. A green up arrow helps, a red down arrow hurts, and a diamond cuts both ways. Gold is the diamond. Tax and GST changes carry a green arrow because the row is framed around a cut lifting spending a quarter later.
  • Weight: one to three dots. Only two rows carry three: food inflation and gold.

The last column shows today's reading where a dial maps to a series we track: food inflation, the gold price, the money-market rate, the realty index as a proxy for commercial rents, clothing and footwear inflation as a proxy for garment costs, and consumer non-durables output. Wage growth shows general consumer inflation, the closest series we track. Tax changes and quick-commerce growth show a dash, so follow those through the news.

Use the table door by door. For a grocer, read food inflation, quick commerce and non-durables output. For a fashion chain, food inflation, tax changes and rent. For a jeweller, gold above all, then the wedding calendar from card three. The so-what line gives the two to track if you track nothing else: food inflation for fashion and grocery, gold for jewellery.

c7.story:
Indian retail has the longest runway of almost any industry: organised chains still hold well under a fifth of the market. So why has it taken decades rather than years to grab that share? Because the bottlenecks are real, and two of them are permanent.

The first is the kirana itself. It is easy to underestimate. A neighbourhood shop has almost no rent because the owner often lives upstairs, no salaried staff beyond the family, and a relationship that lets regular customers buy on credit and pay at month-end. It delivers to your door, and it has done so for decades. Organised retail wins on range, price and experience, but it is fighting a rival with almost no costs.

The second structural force is newer: quick commerce. Blinkit, Zepto and Instamart deliver in minutes from dark stores, and they are taking exactly the purchases that used to justify a trip to a big store, the forgotten milk, the impulse snack, the top-up basket. For urban grocery chains this is a permanent change in how people shop.

Then the slow constraint: good locations. High-footfall sites in big cities are scarce and expensive, so growth must move to smaller towns, which is exactly where Zudio and Vishal Mega Mart have been opening.

And then the recurring risks that hit specific quarters. Inventory risk: a fashion season that misses, or a gold price fall, leaves stock that must be discounted. Gold regulation: hallmarking, import duties and cash limits can change jewellery economics overnight. When the July 2024 Union Budget cut gold import duty sharply, jewellers holding expensive inventory took a hit on its value even as the cut promised more demand. Talent: trained store managers are scarce and attrition is high. And seasonality: festive and wedding seasons dominate, so a Diwali that falls in a different month can make one quarter look brilliant and the next look broken.
c7.read:
Each row is one bottleneck, with why it bites and a severity label. The label tells you how to think about the risk.

  • Structural: permanent. Two rows here, and they pull in opposite directions in a useful way. Unorganised competition is the reason the runway is so long, and also the reason share gains are slow. Quick-commerce disruption is the new permanent rival in urban grocery. Both belong in your valuation.
  • Slow: good store locations. Scarce in big cities, which is pushing expansion to small towns over years.
  • Recurring: four rows. Inventory risk, gold regulation, talent and seasonality. These are the quarter-level risks: a missed season, a duty change, a wave of attrition, a shifted Diwali.

Read the table door by door. A value grocer cares most about the two structural rows and location costs. A fashion chain cares about inventory risk and talent. A jeweller cares about gold regulation and the wedding calendar. A distributor barely appears on this table at all, because its risks are dealer credit and product cycles rather than shop-floor issues.

The so-what line puts it in one sentence: unorganised share is the long runway, quick commerce is the new threat, and inventory and gold rules are the quarter-level risks. A useful habit is to set a news alert for any change in gold import duty or hallmarking rules if you hold a jeweller, and to read the inventory note in every fashion chain's results before the revenue line.

c8.story:
Retail is not a heavily licensed industry, but a handful of rules shape it more than you might expect, and the gold rules most of all.

Start with hallmarking. For most of Indian history, buying gold jewellery meant trusting the jeweller about its purity. Some local jewellers sold gold that was a little purer on the bill than in the metal. From June 2021, BIS hallmarking became mandatory in phases, and a unique hallmark identification number on every piece followed in 2023. The rule did something powerful for organised chains: it made purity verifiable, and once a shopper can check, the trust gap between a local shop and Kalyan narrows in a way that favours the chain with the bigger brand and the cleaner record.

Then gold duty. The July 2024 Union Budget cut customs duty on gold sharply. Cheaper gold lifts demand and weakens the incentive for smuggling, which had long undercut honest jewellers. But a sudden cut also lowers the value of inventory jewellers already hold, a one-off hit worth watching for in that quarter's results.

The GST Council sets rates on clothes, footwear, groceries and gold, and the September 2025 cut on clothes and daily goods was a direct price cut for shoppers. RBI's rules on gold and metal loans decide how cheaply a jeweller can carry stock.

FDI policy is the quiet rule shaping the battlefield. India limits foreign ownership in multi-brand retail and bars inventory-led e-commerce by foreign-owned platforms. That is why Amazon and Flipkart operate as marketplaces rather than owning the goods they sell, and why foreign supermarket chains never arrived in force.

And the rule that could matter most for grocers is still pending: the Competition Commission's examination of quick-commerce discounting and dark stores, following complaints from distributor groups. A ruling that curbs deep discounts would ease pressure on big-box grocery.
c8.read:
Each row is a regulator or rule. Read across: who it is, what it does, why you care, and its status.

  • Live: the GST Council and customs duty on gold. These two can move prices and demand at once, and both have moved recently: GST cuts on clothes and daily goods, and a sharp cut in gold duty in 2024.
  • Always: permanent fixtures. BIS hallmarking, RBI gold-loan rules, FDI policy in retail, Legal Metrology with FSSAI, and the state shops and establishments acts. Most rarely make news, but hallmarking is the one doing slow, steady work for organised jewellers, and FDI policy is why the online giants run as marketplaces.
  • Coming: the Competition Commission's look at online discounting and dark stores. The single most important pending rule for urban grocery.

Map the rows to doors. Jewellers answer to hallmarking, gold duty, RBI metal-loan rules and GST on gold, four rows out of eight, which tells you how regulated their economics really are. Grocers answer to FSSAI, Legal Metrology, the shops acts and the coming competition ruling. Fashion answers mainly to GST. Distributors barely appear.

The state shops and establishments acts deserve a second look: longer permitted opening hours lift sales per store with no extra rent. Dated regulatory news filtered for this industry sits on the Picks and signals tab.

c9.story:
Michael Porter's five forces ask one question: once the money comes in, who gets to keep it? Retail answers differently depending on what is on the shelf.

Start with grocery. Rivalry is brutal. A grocer competes with every kirana in the neighbourhood, with the quick-commerce apps on every phone, and with the other chains. Price is the weapon, and everyone can see everyone else's price. Buyers switch for a few rupees on a basket. Substitutes are multiplying: why drive to a supermarket when the app delivers the same packet in minutes? And suppliers have some power, because the big FMCG brands are must-stock items that a grocer cannot refuse to carry. That leaves the grocer one way to win: be the cheapest and most efficient, year after year. DMart is the proof that it can be done, and the warning about how hard it is.

Now fashion and jewellery. Rivalry is real but fought on brand, design and trust rather than price alone. Suppliers have little power: fashion chains own their brands and contract out the stitching, and jewellers buy gold at the market price like everyone else. Buyers are more loyal, because a shopper who likes how Zudio's clothes fit, or a family that has bought wedding gold from the same jeweller for two generations, does not switch for a small discount. Entrants face years of work: you can open a grocery store or an app quickly, but building a fashion brand or jewellery trust takes a long time. And substitutes are weaker: nobody orders wedding jewellery in ten minutes, and clothes still need a fitting room.

You can open a grocery app in a year. You cannot buy a family's trust in its jeweller in a decade.

The result is a clean ranking: fashion brands and trusted jewellery chains keep more of the profit, and grocery leaders survive by being the most efficient operator in the room.
c9.read:
The radar has five spokes, one per force. The further a shape reaches along a spoke, the more pressure that force exerts. So a smaller shape is the better business.

Two shapes are drawn: value grocery, and fashion and jewellery. Look at size first. The grocery shape is larger on every single spoke, reaching the outer ring on rivalry and pushing far out on buyers and substitutes. The fashion and jewellery shape sits inside it all the way round.

That is worth noticing, because in many industries the two shapes cross somewhere, and here they do not. There is no force on which grocery has the easier life. The gaps are widest on substitutes and buyers, the two spokes quick commerce is enlarging: apps substitute for the store visit, and shoppers comparing app prices switch more readily.

The narrowest gaps are on suppliers and entrants. On suppliers both shapes sit close to the centre. Grocers face some power from must-stock FMCG brands; fashion chains own their brands and jewellers buy gold at market, so neither door is badly squeezed from that side.

The table beside the radar gives each score from zero, no pressure, to three, heavy pressure, with a one-line reason. To use it on a single company, start from its door's shape and adjust. A value grocer that owns its stores and buys at scale is pushing its supplier and rivalry spokes inward through sheer efficiency. A distributor, not drawn here, would sit even further out than grocery on rivalry and buyers. If you disagree with a reason for a company you hold, redraw its shape; that is how the framework is meant to be used.

c10.story:
A retail results call is full of store openings, festive campaigns and new formats. Underneath, eight numbers tell you whether the business is really getting stronger, and three of the most important are not in the financial statements at all.

Same-store sales growth comes first. It measures sales growth at stores open for more than a year, stripping out the effect of new openings. A chain can post handsome headline growth simply by opening lots of stores while every existing store sells less than last year. Same-store sales tell you whether shoppers actually want more of what you sell.

Then the growth engine: store additions and square feet. This is the runway being used, and it comes with a test, the payback period on a new store. A chain that adds area quickly and earns back each store's cost within a few years can compound for a long time. One that adds area while payback stretches is building a problem.

Revenue per square foot is the productivity check. As new stores mature, it should hold or rise. If it falls across the estate, the chain is opening stores in places that cannot support them, or the format is tiring.

Then the financial trio. Gross margin shows pricing power and discounting: in fashion, a falling gross margin usually means the chain is clearing stock it could not sell at full price. EBITDA margin shows how efficiently the stores run. Inventory days tell you how fast stock turns, with very different benchmarks for a grocer, a fashion chain and a jeweller.

Finally, sales growth and return on capital. Headline sales growth combines stores and demand, so always read it next to same-store sales. And return on capital tells you whether the stores earn back what they cost, which is the only thing that justifies opening more of them.
c10.read:
The table has one row per number. Read across: the number, what it tells you, what good looks like, and today's industry median.

  • What it tells you is the question to ask. Read the first three rows as one block, demand, expansion and productivity, then the financial rows.
  • What good looks like is the benchmark, and here it splits clearly by door: separate marks for grocery, fashion and jewellery on gross margin, EBITDA margin and inventory days. A jeweller holding far more inventory than a grocer is normal; a grocer holding like a jeweller would be alarming. Always compare a company with its own door's mark.
  • Today's industry median comes from the latest annual filings of the industry's listed companies in our database. It appears for gross margin, EBITDA margin, inventory days, sales growth and return on capital. Same-store sales, store additions and revenue per square foot show a dash, because companies report them in presentations and calls rather than in a standard line.

A caution specific to retail: the median mixes grocers, fashion chains, jewellers and thin-margin distributors, so it can land somewhere no real company sits. Treat it as a weather report for the label, not a target. The better comparison is three-way: the company's own number, its door's good mark, and its own trend. And always read the first row before the seventh: headline sales growth without same-store sales is half a story.

c11.story:
The best warnings about a retail quarter do not come from the retailers. They come from the vegetable market, the bullion screen, the priest's calendar, the Union Budget and the leasing desks of mall developers.

The earliest voices speak two quarters ahead. Rural wage and farm income data tell you what small-town households will spend after the harvest, and small towns are where the chains are opening. Mall and high-street leasing tell you where stores will open next: a lease signed today is a store trading in two quarters, and a slowdown in leasing is the earliest hint that a chain is turning cautious.

One quarter ahead, a cluster of signals. The food inflation print: lower inflation frees spending for fashion and gold a quarter later. The wedding and festive calendar: auspicious dates decide which quarter gets the sales. Tax changes in the budget or the GST Council: disposable income lifts the next quarter's spending. And quick-commerce order growth, which tells you how much of the urban grocery basket is moving to apps.

And one signal hits immediately: the gold price. Jewellery revenue and volumes react within the same quarter.

Combine them and you get the rule. The industry is in an up-cycle when same-store sales are accelerating, food inflation is easing, and store expansion is holding returns. Today two of three tick: festive demand is strong and food inflation is moderate after the tax relief. The third does not: new stores are diluting margins, as rapid expansion into new towns usually does in its first years. Two out of three reads as recovery. That is why the call leans towards value fashion and organised jewellery chains taking share from local shops, and stays selective in urban grocery, where quick commerce keeps squeezing.

The chart places each outside signal by how far ahead it speaks. The further right a dot sits, the earlier the warning. Hover a dot to read the channel.

  • Far right, two quarters ahead: rural wages and farm income, and mall and high-street leasing. One is a demand signal for small towns, the other an expansion signal. Both speak before anything shows up in results.
  • The middle, one quarter ahead: the food inflation print, the wedding and festive calendar, tax changes, and quick-commerce order growth. Three of these are wallet signals; quick commerce is the competition signal.
  • Far left, the same quarter: the gold price. It does not warn; it tells a jeweller's quarter as it happens.

Use the chart as a reading order: check the right-hand dots first to see where demand and store openings are heading, then the middle to see which quarter will catch the spending, and let gold tell you what is happening in jewellery now.

Below the chart sits the three-sign rule. Two ticks: same-store sales accelerating, with festive demand strong, and food inflation easing, moderate after the tax relief. One cross: expansion holding returns, with the note that new stores dilute margins. Two of three reads as recovery.

The call box gives the view, its three points, and what would change it: a food inflation spike that eats discretionary spending, a gold price crash that hits jewellery inventory values, and quick-commerce apps cutting prices further to win share. Treat those three as alerts; if one appears in the news, the call is due for a rethink.
